h1: Comparing whisky age statements side by side
title: Comparing Whisky Age Statements | Craft Beer School
desc: How to taste whisky age statements side by side: what changes from 10 to 12 to 18 years, why older is not always better and how to set up the flight.
teaser: A 12 and an 18 from the same distillery, side by side. Here is what the extra six years actually bought.
standfirst: Age statements are among the few hard numbers on a whisky label. Tasting different ages from one distillery side by side shows what time in oak really does and where it stops helping.
sections:
The age on a whisky label is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. A 12 year old Scotch may contain much older whisky, but nothing younger than 12 years in the cask. This rule applies to Scotch, Irish whiskey and most other major categories.

Age counts time in the cask, not time in the bottle. A 12 year old bottled in 2010 is still a 12 year old today. Our guide to whisky age statements explained covers the rules in full.

In broad terms, longer time in oak tends to bring:

  • More wood flavour: vanilla, toffee, spice, then drier tannic notes.
  • Less raw spirit: fewer sharp, grainy or new make notes.
  • Oxidation: slow reactions through the wood that create fruitier, more complex notes such as dried fruit, polish and old leather.
  • Deeper colour: from the wood, though caramel colouring can mask this.
  • Softer peat: smoke tends to fade with age, so an older Islay malt is usually less smoky than a young one.

None of these is guaranteed. The cask type, its previous fills and where it sat in the warehouse matter as much as the years.

There is a sweet spot for every spirit and cask combination. Past it, the wood starts to dominate and the whisky becomes dry, bitter or tired. A delicate spirit in an active cask may peak young. A heavy spirit in a refill cask may need decades.

Climate changes the clock. In Scotland, maturation is slow and evaporation is commonly quoted at around 2% a year. In Indian heat the whisky works through the wood much faster and loses far more to evaporation. Our guide to the angel's share in Indian heat explains why. A 6 year old Indian malt may taste as mature as a much older Scotch, which is why many Indian single malts carry no age statement at all.

The best age comparison uses whiskies from the same distillery and ideally the same cask style, so age is the main variable. Many distilleries sell a core range such as 10, 12, 15 and 18 years old, which makes a natural flight.

  • Pour 15 to 20 ml of each into identical tulip glasses.
  • Taste youngest to oldest. Older whiskies often have stronger wood and longer finishes that would mask a younger one tasted afterwards.
  • If the strengths differ, note it. A 46% 10 year old will feel fuller than a 40% 12 year old, regardless of age.
  • Have water for drinking and for adding to the glass.

For a sharper test, ask someone to pour the flight blind and see if you can put them in age order. Our guide to tasting whisky blind explains how.
What to look for, glass by glass

On the nose, compare how much of the spirit you can still smell. The youngest glass often shows fresh fruit, cereal and some sharpness. Older glasses move towards dried fruit, honey, wood and spice.

On the palate, compare texture and wood grip. Older whiskies often feel rounder and more integrated. The oldest may also feel drier from tannin.

On the finish, compare length and how it ends. A long finish that turns bitter is a sign the wood has gone too far. A long finish that stays sweet and layered is a sign it has not.
Watch the price against the change

Older whiskies usually cost much more, partly because so much stock is lost to evaporation and partly because the distiller has waited years for the money. The tasting tells you whether the difference matters to you.

Many experienced tasters end up with a favourite age in the middle of a range rather than at the top. That is a perfectly sensible result. Price follows scarcity. Your palate follows flavour.

Judging how integrated a whisky feels, rather than just how much oak it shows, is a skill that develops with guided comparison. It is the same skill a brewer uses to judge whether a lager has finished conditioning.
Taste two ages before buying the third

Your first step: buy or share two ages from one distillery, perhaps the 10 or 12 and the next one up. Taste them side by side, youngest first. Write down what changed. If the older one does not taste worth the gap to you, you have just saved money on the next bottle. Sip slowly, drink water and never drink and drive.
faqs: What does the age on a whisky label mean?
It is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle, counted in years in the cask.
Does whisky keep ageing in the bottle?
No. Ageing happens in the cask. A sealed bottle stays essentially the same age.
No. Every spirit and cask has a peak. Past it, the wood can make the whisky dry or bitter.
What order should I taste different ages in?
Youngest to oldest, so the stronger wood of older whiskies does not mask the younger ones.
